lesson.title: When should it switch?
lesson.subtitle: Thresholds, false alarms, and a fan that doesn't flicker

video.title: When should it switch?
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma — maths teacher, the student's teacher (main character)
Mr Okafor — science teacher, the student's teacher (cameo)
Amina Bello — teacher, the student's teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Ms Salma in the school yard beside the water tank; a small alarm box on the tank keeps beeping while pupils walk past.
scenes.animation: The alarm light blinks; heads turn less each time; then the tap runs dry.
scenes.narration: Our school's new tank alarm beeped six times on Monday, and every time the tank was fine. By Wednesday, nobody even looked up. On Thursday the tank really ran dry, and nobody listened. The rule was fine; the number in it was wrong.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: choosing the moment a device should switch.

scenes.visual: A thermometer with a bold line drawn across it at 30; below the line the fan is still, above it the fan spins.
scenes.animation: The mercury rises past the line and the fan starts.
scenes.narration: The number in a rule is its threshold. In fan on above thirty degrees, thirty is the threshold. On one side the device rests; cross it, and the device acts.

scenes.visual: A bar chart of the tank's lowest level each day: five days around 30–36 %, then one day at 12 %.
scenes.animation: Bars rise one by one; the last one stays short and turns red.
scenes.narration: First, look at real readings. On normal days the tank never fell below thirty percent; when the pump broke, it dropped to twelve. So the alarm belongs between the two: about twenty percent.

scenes.visual: Two panels: an alarm ringing over a full, calm tank; a silent alarm over an empty tank.
scenes.animation: A slider between them moves; one panel grows as the other shrinks.
scenes.narration: Any alarm can make two kinds of mistake. A false alarm: it goes off, but nothing is wrong. A miss: something is wrong, but it stays quiet. Move the threshold to cut one, and you usually get more of the other.

scenes.visual: A smoke alarm on a kitchen ceiling beside a phone inbox with a spam folder.
scenes.animation: Each side tilts on a scale as its costly mistake is named.
scenes.narration: Which costs more depends on the job. A smoke alarm that misses a fire could cost lives, so it goes off easily. A spam filter is the opposite: hiding a real message is worse than letting spam through.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor in the school kitchen pointing at a gas alarm above the cooker. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A gas alarm in the school kitchen. Should it go off easily, or only when it's very sure?

scenes.visual: The gas alarm sounds and the kitchen is cleared; then a row of ignored alarms fades.
scenes.animation: Cards appear as each point is said.
scenes.narration: Easily. A missed gas leak could hurt people, so a few false alarms are a fair price. But keep them few, or people stop listening, like our tank alarm.

scenes.visual: A ceiling fan that starts and stops again and again while a thermometer wobbles around 30.
scenes.animation: On, off, on, off, faster each time.
scenes.narration: Now a new problem. A fan rule says on above thirty degrees, off below thirty. The room hovers right at thirty, so the fan clicks on and off all lesson, and wears itself out.

scenes.visual: The thermometer now has two lines, at 30 and 28, with a shaded gap; the fan runs steadily until the room drops below 28.
scenes.animation: The gap shades in; the fan runs smoothly, then stops once.
scenes.narration: The fix is two thresholds with a gap. Fan on above thirty degrees, but off only below twenty-eight; in between, nothing changes. A tank pump works the same way: on below twenty percent, off above ninety.

scenes.visual: Amina beside the school tank; the pump's switch clicks on and off. Two fix cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A tank pump switches on below fifty percent and off above fifty, and it clicks on and off all day. What's the best fix?

scenes.visual: Three cards line up: a chart, a balance scale, two lines on a thermometer.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Two thresholds: on below twenty percent, off above ninety, so the pump fills the tank in one go. Remember: choose thresholds from real readings. Ask which mistake costs more. And use two thresholds to stop the flicker.

scenes.visual: A student in a kitchen with a phone stopwatch, listening to a fridge hum and stop.
scenes.animation: The stopwatch ticks; a small table of run and rest times fills in.
scenes.narration: Try it this week: find a device at home that switches itself, like a fridge or a water heater. Don't open it; just listen, and time how long it runs and rests. If it never flickers, it probably uses two thresholds.

checkpoints.prompt: A gas alarm in the school kitchen: should it go off easily, or only when it's very sure?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a missed gas leak could hurt people, so a few false alarms are worth it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — waiting until it's very sure means more misses, and a missed gas leak could hurt people. Here a miss costs far more.

checkpoints.prompt: A pump goes on below 50% and off above 50%, and clicks on and off all day. What's the best fix?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — two thresholds with a wide gap: the pump fills the tank in one go, then rests.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — one threshold flickers wherever you put it. Two thresholds with a gap stop the flicker.
